newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spanish job reforms trickle into jobs market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spanish job reforms trickle into jobs market.

text.p: Reforms aimed at modernising Spain's rigid labour market have already begun to kick in but are unlikely to touch the swollen unemployment rate, analysts said on Thursday.
A breakdown of jobs data suggest the reforms, introduced in May, have begun to change the structure of the labour market but are not helping create new jobs.

The economy ministry said the first signs of a shift away from temporary to permanent contracts were reflected in June data, showing that employers are opting for more stability -- a key aim of the reforms.
But government promises that the reforms would help to cut Spain's towering unemployment rate -- the highest in Europe -- are unlikely to materialise, analysts said.

"Whilst conceding the (reform) deal is a step in the right direction, it is not signficant or radical enough to make for a dramatic near-term decline in unemployment," said William Thornhill, senior economist at Technical Data.

The government named 1997 Year of the Job and encouraged employers and unions to agree reforms that would inject new life into Spain's stagnant labour market and prepare it for Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU).

The reforms finally adopted included a new permanent contract with lower redundancy costs aimed at improving flexibility in a market where employers have long been hamstrung by high severance pay and easily abused temporary contracts.

But at the end of the day, analysts said the reform deal had been largely political, aimed at placating the unions. They said employers and unions failed to agree anything radical enough to tackle a jobless rate which persists at above 20 percent, according to data from the National Statistics Institute (INE).

"The labour reforms were quite modest and I don't expect any major impact on unemployment," said Jose Luis Alzola, analyst at Salomon Brothers in London. "There may just be some change in the structure of employment with some reduction in temporary jobs and a rise in permanent ones."
A breakdown of jobs data reveals exactly this.

The economy ministry reported that of a total 819,548 contracts in June, 89.2 percent were temporary and 3.9 percent were permanent. This compares to 93 percent and 3.4 percent respectively a year earlier.
Economy ministry data also suggest that the jobless rate is falling, although this is unlikely to be a factor of the reforms, analysts said.

"The fall in the jobless rate is basically due to an economic recovery and not the labour reforms. The seasonally adjusted decline in the jobless rate is similar to the average for the previous five months," said Alzola.

The economy ministry produces alternative jobless data which are significantly lower that the INE data. Analysts say unemployment is probably somewhere between the two taking into account black market jobs.
The ministry said the jobless rate fell to 13.06 percent in June from 13.26 percent a month earlier. The total number unemployed fell to 2.09 million from 2.12 million.
The latest INE data based on a survey completed on a quarterly rolling basis, reported that unemployment had slipped 0.12 points to 21.37 percent from February to April.
Analysts said the INE rate was unlikely to break 20 percent within the next two years without further reforms.
"What the labour market needs is more flexibility and more radical changes in terms of lower firing costs, wage settlement processes and the strong hold of unions," an analyst at a Spanish bank said.

The key problem, analysts say, is that Spain's labour market remains stifled by a framework fundamentally unchanged since the 1970s when the dictatorship of General Francisco Franco promised jobs for life.

While reforms introduced during the transition to democracy brought changes such as collective bargaining, free unions and the recognition of the right to strike, the market remains one of the most rigid in Europe.
